title: Biomaterials
description: A biomedical-engineering biomaterials course moving from material classes and interfaces to host response, mechanics, degradation, manufacturing, regulatory evidence, and design synthesis.

topics.title: Biomaterials Field Overview, Medical-Device Context, and Design Requirements
topics.description: Define biomaterials, device indications, clinical constraints, and design inputs for medical implants and devices.

children.title: Biomaterial Definitions and Device Context
children.description: This subtopic clarifies what counts as a biomaterial and why the same material can perform differently across device contexts.

children.title: Biomaterial versus biological material
Medical device, implant, scaffold, dressing, and diagnostic interface
Intended use, indication, contraindication, and patient population
Temporary, permanent, external communicating, and implantable contact categories
Design Inputs, Use Environment, and Performance Criteria
children.description: The point is to translate clinical need into measurable engineering requirements before choosing a material.

children.title: Design input, design output, verification, and validation
Use environment: pH, enzymes, oxygen, salts, temperature, and motion
Mechanical load case, fluid exposure, tissue contact, and service life
Risk controls, failure modes, and acceptance criteria
Medical-Device Examples and Trade-Off Thinking
children.description: Examples help students see biomaterials as design choices with benefits, compromises, and constraints.

children.title: Hip stem, dental implant, vascular graft, stent, catheter, contact lens, and wound dressing
Biocompatibility versus mechanical strength
Degradation versus long-term stability
Manufacturability, cost, sterilization, and regulatory evidence

topics.title: Materials Classes Used in Medicine: Polymers, Metals, Ceramics, and Composites
topics.description: Compare the major materials families used in medicine and match their properties to device functions.

children.title: Polymers and Elastomers
children.description: Students learn why soft, processable materials dominate many flexible devices and drug-delivery systems.

children.title: Thermoplastic, thermoset, elastomer, hydrogel, and biodegradable polymer
Polyethylene, Polyurethane, Silicone, PMMA, PLA, PGA, PLGA, and PEG
Glass-transition temperature, crystallinity, molecular weight, and chain mobility
Additives, plasticizers, leachables, and extractables
Metals and Alloys
children.description: Metals matter because load-bearing implants require strength, fatigue resistance, and corrosion control.

children.title: Titanium alloys, stainless steel, cobalt-chromium, tantalum, magnesium, and nitinol
Elastic modulus, yield strength, fracture toughness, and fatigue strength
Passivation layer, galvanic couple, pitting corrosion, and fretting corrosion
Shape-memory effect and superelasticity in nitinol
Ceramics, Glasses, and Composites
children.description: This section shows how brittle, bioactive, or composite materials can solve problems that polymers and metals cannot solve alone.

children.title: Alumina, zirconia, hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, and bioactive glass
Brittleness, hardness, wear resistance, and fracture toughness
Bioinert, bioactive, and resorbable ceramics
Fiber reinforcement, particle reinforcement, and matrix-interface bonding

topics.title: Surface Chemistry, Wettability, and Protein Adsorption
topics.description: Explain how surface energy, chemistry, topography, and adsorbed proteins shape early biological response.

children.title: Surface Energy and Wettability
children.description: The gist is that biology first encounters the surface, not the bulk material.

children.title: Contact angle, hydrophilicity, hydrophobicity, and surface energy
Polar, nonpolar, charged, and zwitterionic functional groups
Roughness, topography, nanoscale texture, and surface area
Surface treatment, plasma activation, silanization, and grafting
Protein Adsorption and Protein Corona
children.description: Students learn that adsorbed proteins often mediate the first biological conversation between a material and tissue.

children.title: Albumin, fibrinogen, fibronectin, collagen, vitronectin, and immunoglobulins
Adsorption kinetics, desorption, denaturation, and competitive exchange
Vroman effect and changing protein layers over time
Protein corona around nanoparticles and particulate biomaterials
Surface Characterization Methods
children.description: Measurement tools give students evidence for claims about surface chemistry and biological response.

children.title: Contact-angle goniometry
X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy and Elemental Composition
Atomic force microscopy and surface roughness
Scanning electron microscopy and topographic imaging

topics.title: Cell-Material Interactions and Tissue Integration
topics.description: Connect extracellular matrix cues, cell adhesion, cytocompatibility, and tissue integration to biomaterial performance.

children.title: Cell Adhesion and Extracellular Matrix Cues
children.description: This subtopic explains how cells read adsorbed proteins, ligand patterns, and matrix-like signals.

children.title: Integrins, focal adhesions, actin cytoskeleton, and mechanotransduction
RGD Peptide, Collagen, Laminin, Fibronectin, and Glycosaminoglycans
Cell attachment, spreading, migration, proliferation, and differentiation
Ligand density, stiffness, and topographic guidance
Cytocompatibility and Cell Assays
children.description: Students need to know how cell-based tests generate early evidence of material safety and function.

children.title: Cytotoxicity, viability, proliferation, apoptosis, and necrosis
MTT, Resazurin, Live/Dead Staining, LDH Release, and Microscopy
Direct-contact, extract, and indirect-contact assay formats
Positive control, negative control, dose, exposure time, and interpretation limits
Tissue Integration and Remodeling
children.description: The goal is to connect cell behavior to longer-term integration or isolation of an implanted material.

children.title: Osteointegration, endothelialization, epithelialization, and soft-tissue integration
Fibroblast activity, collagen deposition, matrix remodeling, and scar formation
Macrophage phenotype, tissue ingrowth, and vascularization
Integration versus encapsulation versus rejection

topics.title: Biocompatibility, Inflammation, and Host Response
topics.description: Analyze acute and chronic tissue responses, foreign body reaction, hemocompatibility, and immune compatibility.

children.title: Inflammation and Foreign Body Reaction
children.description: This subtopic helps students trace the classic sequence from injury to repair, chronic inflammation, or encapsulation.

children.title: Hemostasis, clotting, complement activation, and acute inflammation
Neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, fibroblasts, and foreign body giant cells
Chronic inflammation, granulation tissue, fibrous capsule, and foreign body reaction
Resolution, scarring, integration, and implant isolation
Hemocompatibility and Thrombosis
children.description: Blood-contacting materials require special attention because small surface differences can trigger clotting.

children.title: Platelet adhesion, platelet activation, thrombus formation, and embolic risk
Coagulation cascade, intrinsic pathway, extrinsic pathway, and fibrin formation
Hemolysis, complement, leukocyte activation, and endothelial response
Anticoagulant coatings, heparinization, and nitric-oxide-releasing surfaces
Biological Evaluation Endpoints
children.description: Students learn the vocabulary used to decide which biological safety tests belong in a device evidence plan.

children.title: Cytotoxicity, sensitization, irritation, acute systemic toxicity, and subchronic toxicity
Genotoxicity, implantation, pyrogenicity, and hemocompatibility
Material-mediated pyrogen, extractables, leachables, and degradation products
Risk-Based Endpoint Selection Under ISO 10993 Logic

topics.title: Mechanical Properties, Viscoelasticity, Wear, and Fatigue
topics.description: Use engineering mechanics to evaluate stiffness, strength, toughness, creep, fatigue, and wear in biomaterials.

children.title: Stress-Strain Behavior
children.description: The point is to read mechanical curves as evidence of whether a material can survive its intended load.

children.title: Stress, strain, elastic modulus, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation
Toughness, resilience, ductility, brittleness, and fracture strain
Compression, tension, bending, torsion, and shear tests
Anisotropy, strain rate, hydration, and temperature effects
Viscoelasticity, Creep, and Relaxation
children.description: Soft biomaterials and tissues often respond over time, so students need time-dependent mechanics.

children.title: Elastic response, viscous response, hysteresis, and damping
Creep, stress relaxation, dynamic mechanical analysis, and storage/loss modulus
Maxwell, Kelvin-Voigt, and standard linear solid models
Hydrogel swelling, polymer chain mobility, and tissue-like mechanics
Fatigue, Wear, and Particulate Debris
children.description: Long-lived implants can fail after repeated loads or wear even when single-load strength looks adequate.

children.title: S-N Curve, Fatigue Limit, Crack Initiation, Crack Propagation, and Fracture Surface
Abrasive wear, adhesive wear, fretting wear, and third-body wear
Wear debris, polyethylene particles, osteolysis, and macrophage activation
Tribology, lubrication, articulation surfaces, and simulator testing

topics.title: Degradation, Corrosion, Resorption, and Long-Term Stability
topics.description: Predict how polymers, metals, ceramics, and composites change in the body over time.

children.title: Polymer Degradation and Erosion
children.description: Students learn how degradable materials lose mass, strength, and function over clinically relevant time scales.

children.title: Hydrolysis, enzymatic degradation, oxidation, and chain scission
Bulk erosion, surface erosion, autocatalysis, and mass loss
PLA, PGA, PLGA, Polycaprolactone, and Biodegradable Sutures
Degradation products, local pH, inflammatory response, and mechanical retention
Metal Corrosion and Passivation
children.description: The goal is to understand why corrosion control is central to implant safety and longevity.

children.title: Passivation layer, oxide film, breakdown potential, and repassivation
Pitting corrosion, crevice corrosion, galvanic corrosion, and fretting corrosion
Ion release, nickel sensitivity, cobalt/chromium concerns, and inflammatory effects
Electrochemical testing, polarization curves, and simulated body fluid
Ceramic Resorption and Stability
children.description: Ceramics can be stable, bioactive, or resorbable; matching that behavior to the clinical job is the key.

children.title: Hydroxyapatite, tricalcium phosphate, bioactive glass, alumina, and zirconia
Dissolution, resorption, bone bonding, and mineral exchange
Phase stability, transformation toughening, and aging in zirconia
Long-term fixation, brittleness, and particle generation

topics.title: Polymers, Hydrogels, and Soft Biomaterials
topics.description: Study soft and degradable biomaterials used in drug delivery, wound care, scaffolds, and tissue interfaces.

children.title: Polymer Chemistry and Structure
children.description: This section connects molecular design to bulk behavior in soft medical materials.

children.title: Monomer, repeat unit, copolymer, block copolymer, and network polymer
Molecular weight, polydispersity, crystallinity, and glass-transition temperature
Crosslinking, chain entanglement, plasticization, and solvent uptake
Synthetic polymers versus natural polymers such as collagen, gelatin, chitosan, and alginate
Hydrogel Properties
children.description: Hydrogels are useful because their water-rich networks can mimic tissue-like environments.

children.title: Swelling ratio, mesh size, crosslink density, and equilibrium water content
Physical crosslinks, covalent crosslinks, ionic gels, and thermoresponsive gels
PEG, PHEMA, Alginate, Hyaluronic Acid, Collagen, and Fibrin Gels
Diffusion, permeability, mechanical softness, and cell encapsulation
Soft Biomaterial Applications
children.description: Applications make the property-function relationship concrete for students.

children.title: Contact lenses, wound dressings, injectable gels, tissue adhesives, and soft-tissue fillers
Drug depots, microspheres, nanoparticles, and hydrogel release platforms
Sutures, meshes, membranes, and resorbable fixation devices
Sterility, hydration, shelf stability, and handling in clinical use

topics.title: Metals, Ceramics, Coatings, and Hard-Tissue Interfaces
topics.description: Examine load-bearing and hard-tissue materials, including alloys, bioactive ceramics, coatings, and osseointegration.

children.title: Load-Bearing Metallic Implants
children.description: Students see why alloy choice, fatigue behavior, and fixation strategy determine hard-tissue device success.

children.title: Titanium hip stem, cobalt-chromium femoral head, stainless-steel fracture plate, and dental implant
Stress shielding, modulus mismatch, osseointegration, and implant loosening
Surface roughening, porous coating, grit blasting, and additive manufacturing
Nickel-titanium stents and superelastic deformation
Bioactive and Bioinert Ceramics
children.description: This subtopic distinguishes ceramics that bond with tissue from ceramics used mainly for hardness and wear resistance.

children.title: Hydroxyapatite coating, bioactive glass, calcium phosphate cement, alumina, and zirconia
Osteoconduction, bone apposition, and mineralized interface formation
Wear couples in joint replacements and ceramic-on-ceramic articulation
Fracture toughness, flaw sensitivity, and reliability concerns
Coatings and Interface Engineering
children.description: Coatings let engineers tune the interface while preserving favorable bulk properties.

children.title: Plasma-sprayed hydroxyapatite, titanium plasma spray, anodization, and sol-gel coatings
Diamond-like carbon, drug-eluting coatings, and antimicrobial coatings
Coating adhesion, delamination, thickness, roughness, and porosity
Interfacial shear strength, scratch testing, and coating durability

topics.title: Sterilization, Manufacturing, Packaging, and Shelf-Life Constraints
topics.description: Understand how processing, sterilization, packaging, and storage alter material properties and device safety.

children.title: Sterilization Methods and Material Effects
children.description: Students learn that sterilization is not a final checkbox; it can change chemistry, mechanics, and biological response.

children.title: Ethylene oxide, gamma irradiation, electron beam, autoclave, dry heat, and gas plasma
Sterility assurance level, bioburden, endotoxin, and residual sterilant
Polymer chain scission, crosslinking, oxidation, hydrolysis, and embrittlement
Compatibility of hydrogels, coatings, electronics, and drug-loaded devices
Manufacturing and Processing Constraints
children.description: The point is to make material choices that can actually be produced reliably and cleanly.

children.title: Injection molding, extrusion, machining, sintering, electrospinning, casting, and additive manufacturing
Cleanroom, GMP, Process Validation, Lot Traceability, and Contamination Control
Surface finish, dimensional tolerance, residual stress, and post-processing
Scalability, repeatability, yield, and cost constraints
Packaging, Aging, and Shelf Life
children.description: Packaging and storage protect both sterility and material performance until clinical use.

children.title: Sterile barrier system, seal integrity, moisture barrier, oxygen barrier, and labeling
Accelerated aging, real-time aging, temperature, humidity, and light exposure
Leachables, extractables, oxidation, hydrolysis, and package-material interactions
Shelf-life claims, expiration dating, and shipping stress

topics.title: Drug Delivery Materials and Controlled Release
topics.description: Explain how biomaterials control release through diffusion, swelling, erosion, degradation, and device architecture.

children.title: Release Mechanisms
children.description: This subtopic explains how materials turn a dose into a time profile.

children.title: Diffusion-controlled release, swelling-controlled release, degradation-controlled release, and osmotic release
Matrix system, reservoir system, membrane control, and depot formulation
Burst release, lag phase, zero-order release, first-order release, and sustained release
Fickian Diffusion, Higuchi Model, and Erosion-Coupled Transport
Drug Carriers and Form Factors
children.description: Students compare carrier architectures and how they affect payload, release, targeting, and manufacturability.

children.title: Microspheres, nanoparticles, liposomes, micelles, implants, patches, and hydrogels
PLGA Particles, PEGylation, Surface Charge, Particle Size, and Biodistribution
Encapsulation efficiency, drug loading, release medium, and sink conditions
Local delivery versus systemic delivery and passive versus active targeting
Stability, Safety, and Evaluation
children.description: Drug delivery materials must preserve the therapy while avoiding unsafe degradation or dose profiles.

children.title: Protein stability, drug-polymer compatibility, crystallization, and hydrolysis
In vitro release assay, dialysis, sampling schedule, and cumulative release
Sterilization impact on drug potency and carrier integrity
Dose dumping, local toxicity, immune response, and degradation byproducts

topics.title: Implants, Scaffolds, Wound-Healing Materials, and Tissue Engineering
topics.description: Integrate biomaterials with scaffold architecture, tissue ingrowth, wound healing, vascularization, and regeneration.

children.title: Scaffold Design Variables
children.description: The point is to make scaffold architecture serve cell entry, nutrient transport, mechanics, and degradation.

children.title: Porosity, pore size, interconnectivity, tortuosity, and surface area
Fiber diameter, electrospun mat, 3D-printed lattice, and porous foam
Mechanical stiffness, degradation rate, and tissue-specific geometry
Cell seeding, cell infiltration, and matrix deposition
Wound-Healing and Regeneration Concepts
children.description: Students connect material design to hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, remodeling, and tissue repair.

children.title: Hemostatic dressing, moisture balance, exudate control, and oxygen permeability
Inflammatory phase, proliferative phase, granulation tissue, and remodeling phase
Growth factors, morphogen gradients, cytokines, and extracellular matrix signals
Angiogenesis, vascularization, and mass-transport limits
Tissue-Engineering Translation
children.description: This subtopic frames the gap between promising constructs and clinical products.

children.title: Bioreactor, mechanical stimulation, perfusion, and nutrient transport
Autologous cells, allogeneic cells, stem cells, and immunogenicity
Construct characterization, imaging, mechanical testing, and histology
Scale-up, sterility, regulatory classification, and reimbursement constraints

topics.title: Biofilms, Infection Prevention, and Antimicrobial Strategies
topics.description: Analyze microbial adhesion, conditioning films, biofilm formation, and antimicrobial material strategies.

children.title: Microbial Adhesion and Biofilm Formation
children.description: Students learn how device surfaces can become protected microbial communities rather than simple contamination sites.

children.title: Conditioning film, bacterial adhesion, reversible attachment, and irreversible attachment
Extracellular polymeric substance, quorum sensing, microcolonies, and mature biofilm
Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Pseudomonas, and Candida
Antibiotic tolerance, immune evasion, and chronic device infection
Antifouling and Bactericidal Surfaces
children.description: The gist is to compare surfaces that resist attachment with surfaces that actively kill microbes.

children.title: PEG, Zwitterionic Coatings, Superhydrophilic Surfaces, and Low-Fouling Polymers
Silver, copper, antimicrobial peptides, quaternary ammonium groups, and nitric oxide release
Contact-killing surface, eluting coating, and triggered-release system
Cytotoxicity trade-offs, depletion, resistance pressure, and durability
Testing Infection-Prevention Strategies
children.description: Students need evidence tools for judging whether an antimicrobial material really works.

children.title: Zone of inhibition, colony-forming units, live/dead staining, and crystal violet assay
Static Biofilm Model, Flow-Cell Model, CDC Biofilm Reactor, and Animal Infection Model
Sterility testing versus antimicrobial performance testing
Controls, inoculum size, exposure time, and clinically relevant endpoints

topics.title: Testing Standards, ISO 10993, FDA Pathways, and Regulatory Evidence
topics.description: Connect device contact category, biological endpoints, standards, verification tests, and regulatory submissions.

children.title: ISO 10993 Biological Evaluation Logic
children.description: This subtopic gives students a practical framework for selecting biological tests from device contact and risk.

children.title: ISO 10993-1, Biological Evaluation Plan, and Biological Evaluation Report
Contact type: surface, external communicating, and implant
Contact duration: limited, prolonged, and permanent
Endpoint matrix, existing data, chemical characterization, and risk assessment
Device Testing and Verification Evidence
children.description: Regulatory evidence includes much more than one biocompatibility test.

children.title: Mechanical testing, fatigue testing, wear testing, corrosion testing, and degradation testing
Sterility, endotoxin, packaging validation, shelf life, and transport simulation
Chemical characterization, extractables, leachables, and toxicological risk assessment
Bench testing, animal testing, clinical evidence, and post-market surveillance
FDA Pathways and Documentation
children.description: Students learn how biomaterials decisions become part of a submission story.

children.title: 510(k), De Novo, PMA, Predicate Device, and Substantial Equivalence
Design history file, design control, risk management, and verification records
Material change, process change, and biocompatibility re-evaluation
Labeling, instructions for use, contraindications, and warnings

topics.title: Failure Analysis, Materials Selection, and Biomaterials Design Project
topics.description: Synthesize material properties, biological response, manufacturing, and regulation into a defensible design decision.

children.title: Materials Selection Frameworks
children.description: The point is to choose materials with evidence, not preference or familiarity.

children.title: Functional requirements, constraints, objectives, and free variables
Ashby Chart, Property Map, Trade-Off Matrix, and Weighted Decision Matrix
Biological, mechanical, manufacturing, sterilization, regulatory, and cost criteria
Screening, ranking, sensitivity analysis, and justification
Failure Modes and Root Cause Analysis
children.description: Students learn to diagnose failures by linking symptoms to materials, biology, processing, and use conditions.

children.title: Fracture, fatigue, wear, corrosion, delamination, degradation, infection, and loosening
Fractography, explant analysis, microscopy, spectroscopy, and mechanical retesting
Root cause analysis, fishbone diagram, fault tree, and five whys
FMEA: Severity, Occurrence, Detection, and Risk Priority Number
Capstone Biomaterials Design Project
children.description: The project pulls the course together by requiring a defensible material system and evidence plan.

children.title: Clinical need statement, device requirements, and use environment
Candidate materials, surface treatments, and manufacturing route
Biocompatibility plan, mechanical tests, degradation tests, and sterilization plan
Failure analysis, risk controls, regulatory pathway, and final recommendation
